questions.text: What is a nuclear family?

options: Two parents and their dependent children living together
Three or more generations living together
One parent living with their children
A couple where one partner has children from a previous relationship
feedback: That describes an extended family
That describes a lone-parent family
That describes a reconstituted family

questions.solution: A nuclear family is two parents (adults) and their dependent children in one household
questions.hint: It is the 'core' family of parents and children only

questions.text: What is the term for a family in which one or both partners have children from a previous relationship? Give the term.
questions.solution: A reconstituted (blended or step-) family forms when partners bring children from earlier relationships
questions.hint: The family has been 'put back together' in a new form

questions.text: What term describes a family that includes relatives beyond parents and children, such as grandparents, living together or close by? Give the term.
questions.solution: An extended family includes wider relatives such as grandparents, aunts or uncles
questions.hint: The family is 'stretched' beyond parents and children

questions.text: Which sociologist identified four 'universal' functions of the family: sexual, reproductive, economic and educational?

feedback: Parsons named two functions: primary socialisation and stabilisation of adult personalities
Oakley was a feminist who studied housework
Willis studied working-class boys at school

questions.solution: George Murdock (1949) studied around 250 societies and identified these four functions
questions.hint: He was a functionalist who studied hundreds of societies in the 1940s

questions.text: What is the term for a couple living together without being married or in a civil partnership? Give the term.
questions.solution: Cohabitation is a couple living together in a relationship without marrying; it has become much more common
questions.hint: The word means 'living together'

questions.text: What are conjugal roles?

options: The roles children play at school
The jobs people do in the workplace
The roles of partners in a couple, such as housework, childcare and paid work
The roles of grandparents in an extended family

questions.solution: Conjugal roles are the roles of husband and wife (or partners) in the home; they can be joint or segregated
questions.hint: 'Conjugal' refers to marriage or a couple

questions.text: According to Parsons, what are the two 'basic and irreducible' functions of the modern family?

options: Primary socialisation of children and stabilisation of adult personalities

questions.solution: Parsons said the modern family has two key functions: primary socialisation and the stabilisation of adult personalities
questions.hint: One function is about children and one is about adults

questions.text: Which of these describes segregated conjugal roles?

options: Partners have separate roles, such as one earning money and the other doing the housework
Partners share housework, childcare and decision-making
Partners both do the same paid job
feedback: That describes joint conjugal roles

questions.solution: Segregated roles are separate, often split into male breadwinner and female homemaker; joint roles are shared
questions.hint: 'Segregated' means kept apart

questions.text: Which sociologist studied joint and segregated conjugal roles in London families in the 1950s?
questions.solution: Elizabeth Bott (1957) linked joint and segregated conjugal roles to couples' social networks
questions.hint: She is known for 'Family and Social Network'

questions.text: Which of these is a household but NOT a family?

options: A lone parent and their child
A cohabiting couple with their baby

questions.solution: A household is a person or group living at the same address; a family needs people related by kinship, so one person alone is a household only
questions.hint: A family needs more than one person

questions.text: Which feminist sociologist studied housewives in the 1970s and found that few husbands did a large share of the housework? Give the surname.
questions.solution: Ann Oakley (1974) found that housework was still mainly done by women, challenging claims of equal 'symmetrical' families
questions.hint: She wrote 'The Sociology of Housework'

questions.text: What term describes the family teaching children the basic norms and values of society in their early years? Give the term.

feedback.secondary socialisation: Secondary socialisation happens later, through school, peers and the media
feedback.secondary socialization: Secondary socialisation happens later, through school, peers and the media

questions.solution: Primary socialisation happens in the family in early childhood; secondary socialisation comes later through school, peers and the media
questions.hint: It is the first stage of learning society's ways, and it happens at home

questions.text: Sam lives with his mum, his stepdad and his stepdad's daughter. What type of family is this?
questions.solution: Sam's stepdad has brought his daughter from a previous relationship, so this is a reconstituted family
questions.hint: Look for children from a previous relationship

questions.text: In the Khan household, both partners work full-time and share cooking, cleaning and childcare equally. Which term describes their roles?

feedback: Parsons' instrumental role is the breadwinner role, not sharing tasks equally

questions.solution: Sharing tasks equally is an example of joint conjugal roles
questions.hint: Are the tasks shared or separated?

questions.text: A grandmother, her daughter and her granddaughter all live in the same house. What type of family is this?

feedback: A horizontally extended family adds relatives of the same generation, such as aunts or cousins

questions.solution: Three generations living together is a vertically extended family; horizontal extension adds aunts, uncles or cousins
questions.hint: Count the generations: are they stacked up or side by side?

questions.text: Parsons said that in the traditional nuclear family the husband has the 'instrumental' role. What does this mean?

options: Caring for the children and the home
Being the breadwinner who provides for the family financially
feedback: Parsons called this the expressive role

questions.solution: Parsons' instrumental role is the breadwinner role; the expressive role is caring for the family's emotional needs
questions.hint: 'Instrumental' is about getting things done for the family in the outside world

questions.text: A person has several marriages or long-term partners, one after another, but only one at a time. What is this called? Give the term.

feedback.polygamy: Polygamy means more than one partner at the SAME time

questions.solution: Serial monogamy: a series of partners, one at a time, often linked to divorce and remarriage
questions.hint: 'Serial' means one after another

questions.text: Many families today have four generations alive at once but few children in each generation, so the family tree is long and thin. What is this type of family called? Give the term.
questions.solution: The beanpole family (Brannen): many generations but few members in each, so it is tall and thin
questions.hint: Think of the shape of a tall, thin garden cane

questions.text: A survey of households found: married couples 45%, cohabiting couples 18%, lone-parent families 15%, one-person households 22%. What percentage of these households were couples (married or cohabiting)?
questions.solution: Married couples 45% + cohabiting couples 18% = 63%
questions.hint: Add the two types of couple together

questions.text: Divorce rates rose sharply after the Divorce Reform Act 1969 came into force in England and Wales. What change did the Act make?

options: It allowed divorce on the grounds of 'irretrievable breakdown' of the marriage
It allowed only husbands to start a divorce
It made couples wait 20 years before divorcing

questions.solution: The Act made 'irretrievable breakdown' the only ground for divorce, so couples could divorce after a period of separation without proving fault such as adultery
questions.hint: The Act made divorce easier, not harder

questions.text: Fletcher, a functionalist, argued that rising divorce rates do not show that marriage is less valued. What was his reasoning?

options: People no longer marry at all
People now expect more from marriage, so they divorce if it does not meet their high expectations

questions.solution: Fletcher argued that higher expectations of marriage lead to more divorce, but most divorced people remarry, showing marriage is still valued
questions.hint: Think about what people hope to get from marriage today

questions.text: Which reason for the rise in divorce is linked to changes in women's position in society?

options: People now marry younger than in 1900
Divorce has become harder to obtain
More women are in paid work, so fewer are financially dependent on a husband

questions.solution: Women's growing financial independence means they are less likely to stay in an unhappy marriage for financial reasons
questions.hint: Think about women's financial independence

questions.text: Which two feminist sociologists argued in 'Familiar Exploitation' (1992) that men benefit from women's unpaid work in the family? Give the surnames.
questions.solution: Christine Delphy and Diana Leonard argued the family is a patriarchal institution in which men exploit women's labour
questions.hint: One was a French sociologist whose surname begins with D

questions.text: Describe the functionalist view of the family.

rubric.model_answer: Functionalists see the family as a positive institution that meets the needs of society and its members. Murdock said the family performs four universal functions: sexual, reproductive, economic and educational. Parsons argued that the modern nuclear family has two key functions: primary socialisation of children, so they learn society's norms and values, and stabilisation of adult personalities. Parsons also said the isolated nuclear family fits industrial society because it is small and can move to where work is.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: the family is seen as positive and beneficial for society
1 mark: Murdock's four functions (at least two named)
1 mark: Parsons' primary socialisation
1 mark: Parsons' stabilisation of adult personalities or the nuclear family fitting industrial society
(Maximum 4 marks)

questions.solution: Functionalists: the family benefits society — Murdock's four functions; Parsons' primary socialisation and stabilisation of adult personalities
questions.hint: Start with the general view, then use Murdock and Parsons

questions.text: Which statement is a feminist criticism of the functionalist view of the family?

options: It pays too much attention to conflict and inequality
It says the family is always harmful to everyone
It focuses only on extended families
It ignores how the family can benefit men at women's expense
feedback: Functionalists are usually criticised for ignoring conflict, not for focusing on it

questions.solution: Feminists argue functionalists present the family as good for everyone, ignoring inequality such as women's unpaid domestic work
questions.hint: Feminists focus on inequality between men and women

questions.text: Which statement about Murdock's research on the family is accurate?

options: He studied around 250 societies and claimed the nuclear family was universal
He found that the nuclear family existed in no society
He studied only British families in the 1990s
He argued that the family's main role was to support capitalism
feedback: Supporting capitalism is a Marxist idea, not Murdock's

questions.solution: Murdock (1949) looked at around 250 societies and claimed the nuclear family was found in all of them
questions.hint: His study was published in the 1940s

questions.text: Willmott and Young argued that the 'symmetrical family' was becoming more common. Which feature describes it?

options: The husband makes every decision alone
Partners' roles are more similar and they spend more leisure time at home together
Children leave school early to work for the family

questions.solution: In the symmetrical family, roles are more equal (though not identical), and the family is home-centred and nuclear
questions.hint: 'Symmetrical' means both sides are similar

questions.text: According to Marxist sociologists, who mainly benefits from the family?

feedback: Benefiting everyone equally is closer to the functionalist view

questions.solution: Marxists argue the family serves capitalism, e.g. by raising the next generation of workers and acting as a unit of consumption
questions.hint: Marxists link most institutions to the economic system

questions.text: Which sociological perspective argues that the family benefits men at the expense of women, for example through unpaid housework? Give the perspective.

feedback.functionalist: Functionalists see the family as good for everyone
feedback.functionalism: Functionalists see the family as good for everyone
feedback.marxist: Marxists focus on how the family benefits capitalism
feedback.marxism: Marxists focus on how the family benefits capitalism

questions.solution: Feminists such as Oakley and Delphy and Leonard see the family as patriarchal, benefiting men
questions.hint: This perspective focuses on gender inequality

questions.text: Explain two reasons why divorce rates in the UK rose after the 1960s.

rubric.model_answer: First, changes in the law made divorce easier and cheaper. The Divorce Reform Act 1969 allowed divorce for irretrievable breakdown, so couples did not have to prove a fault such as adultery, and legal aid helped people afford it. Second, women's position changed. More women went into paid work, so fewer were financially dependent on a husband and could leave an unhappy marriage. Feminism also raised women's expectations. Other reasons include less stigma (changing attitudes) and secularisation.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: first reason identified (e.g. legal changes)
2 marks: first reason explained with detail (e.g. Divorce Reform Act 1969, irretrievable breakdown)
1 mark: second reason identified (e.g. women's financial independence, less stigma, secularisation)
2 marks: second reason explained with detail
(Maximum 6 marks)

questions.solution: Easier divorce laws (Divorce Reform Act 1969) and women's greater financial independence; also less stigma and secularisation
questions.hint: Pick two reasons, and explain HOW each one made divorce more likely

questions.text: What term describes the unofficial lessons pupils learn at school, such as obeying authority and being punctual? Give the term.

feedback.formal curriculum: The formal curriculum is the subjects that are officially taught
feedback.national curriculum: The National Curriculum is the official list of subjects and content

questions.solution: The hidden curriculum is the norms and values taught through the way school is organised, not through lessons
questions.hint: These lessons are not on the timetable

questions.text: What is meant by 'material deprivation' in education?

options: Lacking money and resources, such as books, a computer or a quiet place to study
Lacking the values and language that schools reward
Being placed in a low set at school
feedback: That describes cultural deprivation

questions.solution: Material deprivation is lacking the physical and financial resources that help with learning
questions.hint: 'Material' means physical things and money

questions.text: What term describes the knowledge, values, language and tastes that give middle-class pupils an advantage at school? Give the term.

feedback.social capital: Social capital means useful contacts and networks
feedback.economic capital: Economic capital means wealth and income

questions.solution: Cultural capital (Bourdieu) is the middle-class knowledge, tastes and attitudes that schools value
questions.hint: It is a kind of 'wealth' made of culture rather than money

questions.text: Which sociologist argued that education creates social solidarity by passing on society's shared norms and values?

feedback: Willis studied working-class 'lads' and their counter-school culture
Becker studied labelling and the 'ideal pupil'
Bowles (with Gintis) was a Marxist critic of education

questions.solution: Émile Durkheim, a functionalist, saw education as passing on shared culture and creating social solidarity
questions.hint: He was a French functionalist writing over a century ago

questions.text: What is the term for placing pupils in classes by ability for ALL of their subjects? Give the term.

feedback.setting: Setting groups pupils by ability separately for each subject
feedback.banding: Banding puts pupils into broad ability bands, usually containing several classes
feedback.mixed ability: Mixed-ability teaching puts pupils of all abilities together

questions.solution: Streaming puts pupils in one ability group for every subject; setting groups them subject by subject
questions.hint: It is like a river with separate channels

questions.text: What is a self-fulfilling prophecy?

options: A prediction that is always proved wrong
A school rule that pupils must follow
A prediction that comes true because people act as if it were true

questions.solution: A self-fulfilling prophecy happens when a label or prediction changes behaviour so that it comes true
questions.hint: The prediction itself causes the result

questions.text: Which pair of Marxist sociologists put forward the 'correspondence principle'?

feedback: Rosenthal and Jacobson studied the self-fulfilling prophecy
Willmott and Young studied the family

questions.solution: Bowles and Gintis (1976) argued that school mirrors (corresponds to) the workplace in capitalist society
questions.hint: Their book was called 'Schooling in Capitalist America'

questions.text: Which statement describes setting?

options: Pupils are grouped by ability separately for each subject
Pupils are grouped by ability for every subject
Pupils of all abilities are taught together
Pupils are grouped only by age
feedback: That describes streaming
That describes mixed-ability teaching

questions.solution: Setting groups pupils by ability in each subject, so a pupil could be in a top set for maths and a lower set for French
questions.hint: Think about whether a pupil could be in different groups for different subjects

questions.text: Which of these is a feature of marketisation in education?

options: Parents being banned from choosing schools
Schools competing for pupils, with results published so parents can compare them
Every school being made exactly the same size

questions.solution: Marketisation brings market forces into education: competition between schools, published results and parental choice
questions.hint: Think of schools behaving like businesses in a market

questions.text: Which law introduced the National Curriculum and national testing, and gave parents more choice of school, in England and Wales?

feedback: The 1944 Act set up the tripartite system and the 11-plus

questions.solution: The Education Reform Act 1988 brought in the National Curriculum, national testing and more parental choice
questions.hint: It was passed in the late 1980s

questions.text: What term describes a system in which people achieve their position in society through their own talent and effort? Give the term.
questions.solution: In a meritocracy, rewards are based on merit (ability and effort), not on background
questions.hint: The word comes from 'merit'

questions.text: What name is given to the process of a teacher attaching a definition to a pupil, such as 'bright' or 'troublemaker'? Give the term.
questions.solution: Labelling is attaching a definition to someone; interactionists say labels can affect how pupils see themselves
questions.hint: Think of putting a tag on someone

questions.text: Ali's teacher believes he is not very clever and gives him easier work. Over time Ali stops trying and his grades fall. What does this example show?
questions.solution: The teacher's low expectation changed how Ali was treated and how he behaved, so the prediction came true
questions.hint: The teacher's belief came true because of how everyone acted

questions.text: A pupil cannot afford the internet at home and has nowhere quiet to do homework. Which factor affecting achievement is this?
questions.solution: Lacking money and resources such as the internet or a quiet space is material deprivation
questions.hint: These are physical and financial problems

questions.text: At a school, pupils must stand when a teacher enters and must not question the head teacher's decisions. Bowles and Gintis would say this teaches what?

options: Obedience to authority, which prepares pupils for work

questions.solution: Bowles and Gintis argued the hidden curriculum teaches obedience and acceptance of hierarchy, preparing pupils for work in capitalism
questions.hint: Think of the correspondence principle: school mirrors the workplace

questions.text: A middle-class family takes their children to museums and theatres and discusses books at home. These children often do well at school. Which concept does this show?
questions.solution: These experiences give the children cultural capital: knowledge and tastes that schools value and reward
questions.hint: These children have gained knowledge and tastes that schools value

questions.text: Pupils placed in a low stream reject the school's values and gain status from their friends by misbehaving. What is the term for such a group? Give the term.
questions.solution: An anti-school subculture rejects school values; Hargreaves linked them to streaming and Willis studied a 'counter-school culture'
questions.hint: It is a group within the school with its own norms, against the school's

questions.text: A head teacher wants her school to rise in the league tables, so she tries to attract high-achieving pupils. Which trend in education does this show? Give the term.
questions.solution: League tables and competition for pupils are features of marketisation
questions.hint: Schools are behaving like businesses competing for customers

questions.text: In one area, 45% of pupils eligible for free school meals achieved grade 4 or above in English and maths, compared with 72% of other pupils. What does this suggest?

options: Free school meals cause higher grades
There was no link between family income and achievement
Every pupil on free school meals failed
Pupils from poorer backgrounds achieved less well, on average
feedback: 45% of these pupils DID achieve grade 4 or above

questions.solution: Free school meals are a sign of low income; the gap (45% vs 72%) suggests a link between poverty and lower achievement
questions.hint: Free school meals are given to pupils from low-income families

questions.text: Rosenthal and Jacobson told teachers that some pupils, who were really chosen at random, were 'spurters' who would make rapid progress. A year later many of them had made greater gains in IQ. What does this support?
questions.solution: Teachers' raised expectations seem to have changed how they treated the pupils, so the prediction came true
questions.hint: The pupils were chosen at random, so what made the difference?

questions.text: Becker found that teachers judged pupils against an image of the 'ideal pupil'. Which pupils were seen as closest to this ideal?
questions.solution: Becker found teachers saw middle-class pupils as closest to the ideal pupil, and labelled working-class pupils less favourably
questions.hint: Think about whose behaviour and language matched what teachers expected

questions.text: Willis studied 12 working-class 'lads' at a secondary school. What did he conclude?

options: They were all labelled as gifted
They all went on to university
Their counter-school culture prepared them for working-class jobs
They were the most obedient pupils in the school

questions.solution: Willis found the lads rejected school ('having a laff'), which ironically prepared them for manual, working-class jobs
questions.hint: The lads rejected school, and Willis linked this to their future work

questions.text: Which Marxist idea says that the way schools are organised mirrors the workplace, for example hierarchy and following rules? Give the term.
questions.solution: Bowles and Gintis's correspondence principle: school relationships correspond to those at work
questions.hint: School and work 'match' each other

questions.text: Explain two ways in which material deprivation can affect a pupil's achievement.

rubric.model_answer: First, a poor diet or cold, damp, overcrowded housing can lead to illness and tiredness, so the pupil misses school or finds it hard to concentrate. Second, low-income families may not afford resources such as a computer, internet access, books, uniform or school trips. Without a quiet place or the right equipment, homework is harder and the pupil may fall behind or feel embarrassed. Older pupils may need part-time jobs, leaving less time to study.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: first way identified (e.g. poor housing or diet)
1 mark: first way explained (e.g. illness or absence leads to lower achievement)
1 mark: second way identified (e.g. cannot afford resources)
1 mark: second way explained (e.g. homework is harder, pupil falls behind)
(Maximum 4 marks)

questions.solution: Poor diet or housing causes illness and absence; lack of resources such as a computer or quiet space makes study harder
questions.hint: Think about health and home conditions, and about money for resources

questions.text: Which statement is a Marxist criticism of the functionalist view of education?

options: Education allocates people to the jobs that best suit their talents
Education teaches the skills needed by the economy
Education reproduces class inequality rather than giving everyone an equal chance
feedback: This is a functionalist claim, not a criticism of it
This is a functionalist claim (role allocation)

questions.solution: Marxists argue education is not meritocratic: it passes on class inequality from one generation to the next
questions.hint: Marxists focus on social class and inequality

questions.text: Which statement about streaming is supported by studies such as Hargreaves and Ball?

options: Pupils in lower streams or bands were more likely to form anti-school subcultures
Streaming always raises the achievement of every pupil
Streaming has no effect on how teachers treat pupils
Pupils in the top stream usually rejected school values

questions.solution: Hargreaves and Ball found that pupils placed in lower streams or bands were labelled and often formed anti-school subcultures
questions.hint: Think about how pupils react to being placed at the bottom

questions.text: Which statement about labelling theory is accurate?

options: It focuses on how society's large-scale structures are organised
It focuses on small-scale interactions, such as those between teachers and pupils
It argues that teachers' expectations never affect pupils
It was developed by functionalists such as Durkheim

questions.solution: Labelling theory is interactionist: it studies face-to-face interactions and the meanings people give them
questions.hint: Labelling theory comes from the interactionist approach

questions.text: Which is a criticism of the idea that labelling always leads to a self-fulfilling prophecy?

options: It explains every pupil's results perfectly
Some pupils reject a negative label and work harder to prove the teacher wrong
It has never been studied in schools

questions.solution: Labels are not always accepted: some pupils resist them (for example in Fuller's study), so the outcome is not fixed
questions.hint: Do pupils always accept the label they are given?

questions.text: Which sociological perspective, linked to Durkheim and Parsons, sees education as performing positive functions for society as a whole? Give the perspective.

feedback.marxist: Marxists see education as reproducing class inequality
feedback.marxism: Marxists see education as reproducing class inequality
feedback.feminist: Feminists focus on gender inequality in education
feedback.feminism: Feminists focus on gender inequality in education

questions.solution: Functionalists see education as positive: it passes on shared values, teaches skills and allocates roles
questions.hint: This perspective looks at the 'functions' institutions perform

questions.text: Evaluate the view that the education system in the UK is meritocratic.

rubric.model_answer: Functionalists such as Parsons argue education is meritocratic: everyone sits the same exams and is judged by the same standards, and qualifications allocate people to suitable jobs. However, Marxists such as Bowles and Gintis call this a myth: middle-class pupils gain from cultural capital and material advantages, and private schools give extra advantages. Interactionists add that labelling and streaming can hold back working-class pupils. Overall, education rewards achievement, but background still strongly affects who achieves.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: meritocracy explained
1 mark: functionalist argument for the view (e.g. Parsons, same standards)
1 mark: Marxist argument against (e.g. Bowles and Gintis, myth of meritocracy)
1 mark: evidence of class inequality (e.g. cultural capital, material deprivation, private schools)
1 mark: interactionist point (e.g. labelling, streaming)
1 mark: a reasoned conclusion
(Maximum 6 marks)

questions.solution: For: same exams and qualifications (functionalists). Against: class inequality, cultural capital, labelling (Marxists, interactionists)
questions.hint: Give arguments on both sides, then reach a conclusion

questions.text: What is deviance?

options: Behaviour that goes against the norms of a society or group
Behaviour that breaks the law of a country
Behaviour that most people approve of
feedback: That is the definition of crime

questions.solution: Deviance is breaking social norms; crime is breaking the law. Some acts are both
questions.hint: Deviance is about norms, not only laws

questions.text: What term describes the ways a society makes sure people follow its norms, for example through laws, the police or disapproval from family? Give the term.
questions.solution: Social control can be formal (police, courts, laws) or informal (family, friends, gossip, disapproval)
questions.hint: Society 'controls' behaviour in these ways

questions.text: What term describes an exaggerated reaction by the media and the public to a group that is seen as a threat to society? Give the term.
questions.solution: A moral panic: the media exaggerate a threat, creating 'folk devils' and public concern (Stanley Cohen)
questions.hint: Stanley Cohen studied this using the Mods and Rockers

questions.text: Which of these is an example of FORMAL social control?

options: Being told off by a parent

questions.solution: Formal social control is carried out by official agencies such as the police and courts; the others are informal
questions.hint: Formal control comes from official organisations with written rules

questions.text: What is the term for crime that is not reported to the police or not recorded by them? Give the term.
questions.solution: The 'dark figure of crime' is the crime that never appears in police statistics
questions.hint: It is crime we cannot 'see' in the official figures

questions.text: Which sociologist developed strain theory, linking crime to the gap between society's goals and the legitimate means of reaching them?

feedback: Stanley Cohen studied moral panics
Howard Becker developed labelling theory

questions.solution: Robert Merton (1938) argued that strain between goals (such as wealth) and legitimate means can lead to crime
questions.hint: He wrote about the 'American Dream'

questions.text: In Merton's strain theory, which 'adaptation' describes someone who accepts the goal of wealth but uses illegal means, such as theft, to get it?

feedback: Ritualists give up on the goals but keep following the rules
Retreatists reject both the goals and the means
Rebels replace the goals and means with new ones

questions.solution: Innovators accept the goals but reject legitimate means, turning to crime such as theft
questions.hint: This person finds a new (illegal) way to reach the goal

questions.text: In Merton's strain theory, which adaptation describes someone who rejects both society's goals and the legitimate means, and drops out of society?
questions.solution: Retreatists reject both goals and means and withdraw from society
questions.hint: This person 'retreats' from society altogether

questions.text: Which of these is a victim survey that asks people about crimes they have experienced?

options: The Crime Survey for England and Wales

questions.solution: The Crime Survey for England and Wales asks a large sample of people about crimes they have experienced, reported or not
questions.hint: This source asks members of the public directly

questions.text: What is a self-report study?

options: A survey that asks people which crimes they have suffered
A survey that asks people which crimes they have committed
A study of crime stories in newspapers
feedback: That is a victim survey

questions.solution: Self-report studies ask people to admit offences they have committed, often anonymously
questions.hint: The people answering are reporting on themselves

questions.text: Which sociologist wrote 'Folk Devils and Moral Panics' (1972), a study of the Mods and Rockers? Give the surname.
questions.solution: Stanley Cohen showed how media reporting of the Mods and Rockers created a moral panic
questions.hint: His first name was Stanley

questions.text: In labelling theory, what is the term for a label, such as 'criminal', that overrides all of a person's other identities? Give the term.
questions.solution: In labelling theory (Becker), a label such as 'criminal' can become a master status that others see before anything else about the person
questions.hint: It is the 'main' status that dominates the others

questions.text: A teenager sprays graffiti on a wall without the owner's permission. Is this crime, deviance, or both?

options: Deviance only, because no law is broken
Crime only, because nobody disapproves of it
Both crime and deviance, because it breaks the law and social norms

questions.solution: Graffiti without permission is criminal damage (a crime) and also breaks social norms (deviance)
questions.hint: Does it break the law? Does it break social norms?

questions.text: Which of these is deviant but NOT a crime in the UK?

options: Pushing in at the front of a queue

questions.solution: Queue-jumping breaks a social norm, but it is not against the law; the others are crimes
questions.hint: Look for something people disapprove of that is not illegal

questions.text: Newspapers print many stories about 'out-of-control' teenagers after a few fights in a town centre, and politicians call for new laws. Which concept does this show?
questions.solution: Exaggerated media coverage leading to public concern and calls for action is a moral panic
questions.hint: The reaction is much bigger than the events themselves

questions.text: A company director falsifies the company's accounts to avoid paying tax. What type of crime is this?
questions.solution: White-collar crime is committed by people in professional or managerial jobs, often through their work
questions.hint: Think about the kind of job the offender has

questions.text: A young person is caught shoplifting once. Police and teachers then treat them as a 'thief'; they start to see themselves that way and commit more crime. Which theory explains this? Give the theory.
questions.solution: Labelling theory: being labelled can change a person's self-image and lead to more deviance (a deviant career)
questions.hint: The young person was given a name that changed how they saw themselves

questions.text: Which sociologist argued that crime is 'normal' and can be functional for society, for example by reminding people of shared values? Give the surname.
questions.solution: Émile Durkheim, a functionalist, said a certain amount of crime is normal and helps maintain boundaries and allow change
questions.hint: He was a French functionalist who also wrote about education and social solidarity

questions.text: Police recorded 1,200 burglaries in a town, but a victim survey estimated that 2,000 burglaries happened. What percentage of the estimated burglaries did the police record?

feedback: 40% is the share that was NOT recorded (the dark figure)
Divide the smaller number by the larger one

questions.solution: 1,200 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 60%; the other 40% is part of the dark figure
questions.hint: Divide the recorded figure by the estimated total, then multiply by 100

questions.text: Why might official crime statistics underestimate the true amount of crime?

options: Many crimes are never reported to the police or are not recorded by them
The police record every crime that happens
Victims always report crimes straight away
Courts add extra crimes to the figures

questions.solution: Victims may not report crimes (too trivial, fear, distrust) and police may not record them, creating a dark figure
questions.hint: Think about the steps a crime goes through before it appears in the figures

questions.text: Heidensohn argued that women commit less crime than men. Which explanation did she give?

options: Women are naturally more law-abiding for biological reasons
Women face more social control at home, in public and at work
Women are never caught by the police
Women have more legitimate opportunities than men

questions.solution: Heidensohn, a feminist, argued patriarchal social control at home, in public and at work limits women's opportunities to offend
questions.hint: Heidensohn focused on how women's behaviour is controlled

questions.text: Albert Cohen argued that working-class boys who fail at school feel 'status frustration'. What did he say many of them do?

options: Join the police to gain status
Form delinquent subcultures that give them status in other ways
Move abroad to find better jobs

questions.solution: Cohen said these boys form delinquent subcultures with their own values, gaining status through deviance
questions.hint: They find status in a group with different values

questions.text: Which type of study asks people about crimes they have experienced, whether or not they reported them to the police? Give the term.

feedback.self-report study: Self-report studies ask people about crimes they have COMMITTED
feedback.self-report: Self-report studies ask people about crimes they have COMMITTED
feedback.self report study: Self-report studies ask people about crimes they have COMMITTED

questions.solution: Victim surveys, such as the Crime Survey for England and Wales, uncover crime that was never reported
questions.hint: The people asked are those who have suffered crimes

questions.text: Describe Merton's strain theory of crime.

rubric.model_answer: Merton, a functionalist, argued that American society sets everyone the same cultural goal of material success (the American Dream), but not everyone has the same legitimate means, such as education and good jobs, to reach it. This creates strain, or anomie. People adapt in five ways: conformity (accept goals and means), innovation (accept goals but use illegal means, such as theft), ritualism (give up the goals but keep to the rules), retreatism (reject both and drop out) and rebellion (replace goals and means with new ones).
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: society sets shared goals such as wealth
1 mark: not everyone has legitimate means, which creates strain (anomie)
1 mark: innovation explained as the main route to crime
1 mark: at least two other adaptations named or described
(Maximum 4 marks)

questions.solution: Merton: strain between cultural goals (wealth) and legitimate means leads to five adaptations, including innovation (crime)
questions.hint: Start with goals and means, then list the adaptations

questions.text: Which is a Marxist explanation of crime?

options: Crime is caused mainly by biological differences
Crime is functional because it strengthens shared values
Crime happens because women are more controlled than men
Laws are made and enforced in the interests of the ruling class, so working-class crime is targeted more
feedback: That is Durkheim's functionalist view
That is a feminist explanation of women's lower crime rates

questions.solution: Marxists argue the law reflects ruling-class interests, and enforcement focuses on working-class crime more than crimes of the powerful
questions.hint: Marxists focus on social class and capitalism

questions.text: Which is a strength of victim surveys compared with police recorded crime?

options: They include crimes that victims did not report to the police
They include murders and crimes against businesses
They are completely free from memory errors
They record every crime committed in the country
feedback: Murder victims cannot be surveyed, and household surveys mostly miss crimes against businesses

questions.solution: Victim surveys reveal unreported crime; but they cannot include murders, and people may forget or exaggerate
questions.hint: What can a survey of the public find that the police never hear about?

questions.text: Which statement about labelling theory of crime is accurate?

options: It argues that crime is caused by poverty alone
It argues that an act becomes deviant when others label it as deviant
It focuses on how the economy creates crime
It argues that labels have no effect on behaviour
feedback: That is closer to a Marxist approach

questions.solution: Becker argued deviance is not a quality of the act itself but of how others react and label it
questions.hint: Labelling theory looks at reactions to behaviour

questions.text: Which statement about Stanley Cohen's study of the Mods and Rockers is accurate?

options: The media ignored the Mods and Rockers completely
It found that the police caused all of the trouble
Media exaggeration helped create a moral panic and may have increased the deviance it described
It showed that the Mods and Rockers never existed

questions.solution: Cohen found exaggerated reporting created 'folk devils' and may have amplified the behaviour (deviancy amplification)
questions.hint: Think about the effect of media coverage on the groups

questions.text: Which sociological perspective links crime to inequality in capitalist society and argues that the law mainly protects the interests of the powerful? Give the perspective.

feedback.functionalist: Functionalists see some crime as normal and useful for society
feedback.functionalism: Functionalists see some crime as normal and useful for society
feedback.feminist: Feminists focus on gender and crime
feedback.feminism: Feminists focus on gender and crime

questions.solution: Marxists see the law and its enforcement as serving the ruling class
questions.hint: This perspective focuses on capitalism and social class

questions.text: Evaluate the usefulness of official crime statistics.

rubric.model_answer: Official statistics are useful because they are collected regularly, cover the whole country and allow trends over time and comparisons between areas to be studied cheaply. However, they miss the dark figure of crime: many crimes are not reported (too trivial, fear, distrust of police) or not recorded. Police priorities and recording rules can change the figures. Interactionists say they are socially constructed and may reflect police targeting of certain groups. Victim surveys and self-report studies help fill the gaps.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: a strength identified (e.g. large scale, trends over time)
1 mark: the strength explained
1 mark: the dark figure of crime / under-reporting
1 mark: under-recording or police discretion
1 mark: socially constructed (interactionist or Marxist view)
1 mark: a judgement, e.g. useful when combined with victim surveys
(Maximum 6 marks)

questions.solution: Useful for trends and comparisons, but miss the dark figure and are socially constructed; best used with victim surveys
questions.hint: Give strengths first, then weaknesses, then a judgement

questions.text: What term describes data that a sociologist collects for themselves, for example through their own interviews? Give the term.

feedback.secondary data: Secondary data already exists and was collected by someone else
feedback.secondary: Secondary data already exists and was collected by someone else

questions.solution: Primary data is collected first-hand by the researcher, for example through questionnaires, interviews or observation
questions.hint: It is collected first-hand

questions.text: What term describes data that already exists and was collected by someone else, such as government statistics? Give the term.

feedback.primary data: Primary data is collected by the researcher themselves
feedback.primary: Primary data is collected by the researcher themselves

questions.solution: Secondary data comes from existing sources such as official statistics, documents or other researchers' studies
questions.hint: The researcher did not collect it first-hand

questions.text: What is quantitative data?

options: Data in the form of numbers or statistics
Data in the form of words and descriptions
Data that can only be collected by observation
Data that can never come from a questionnaire
feedback: That is qualitative data

questions.solution: Quantitative data is numerical; qualitative data is in words and gives detail and meaning
questions.hint: 'Quantity' means amount

questions.text: What is participant observation?

options: The researcher watches a group from a distance without joining in
The researcher joins in with the group they are studying
Participants fill in a written questionnaire
feedback: That is non-participant observation

questions.solution: In participant observation the researcher takes part in the group's activities while observing them
questions.hint: The researcher becomes one of the 'participants'

questions.text: What is the name for a list of all the members of a target population, from which a sample can be chosen? Give the term.
questions.solution: A sampling frame is a list of the population, such as a school register or the electoral register
questions.hint: It is a list that 'frames' who could be picked

questions.text: What does 'covert' mean in covert participant observation?

options: The group knows they are being studied
The researcher never meets the group
The group does not know they are being studied
feedback: That is overt observation

questions.solution: Covert means secret: the researcher's identity and purpose are hidden from the group
questions.hint: Covert means hidden or secret

questions.text: Which of these is a closed question?

options: How do you feel about school uniform?
Why did you choose your GCSE options?
Do you agree that school uniform should be compulsory? (Yes or No)

questions.solution: Closed questions give a fixed choice of answers, producing quantitative data; open questions let people answer in their own words
questions.hint: A closed question limits the possible answers

questions.text: Which type of interview uses a fixed list of questions asked in the same order to every respondent?

feedback: Unstructured interviews are flexible, like a guided conversation

questions.solution: Structured interviews are standardised, so they are reliable and easy to compare
questions.hint: The questions follow a set 'structure'

questions.text: Which kind of methods do positivist sociologists prefer?

options: Methods that produce rich qualitative data, such as unstructured interviews
Scientific methods that produce quantitative data, such as questionnaires
Methods that collect no data at all
feedback: Interpretivists prefer rich qualitative data

questions.solution: Positivists want sociology to be scientific, using reliable quantitative methods such as questionnaires and official statistics
questions.hint: Positivists want sociology to be like a science

questions.text: What do interpretivist sociologists mainly aim to do?

options: Find laws of society in the way physics finds laws of nature
Understand the meanings people give to their actions
feedback: That is the positivist aim

questions.solution: Interpretivists aim for 'verstehen': understanding meanings, using qualitative methods such as unstructured interviews
questions.hint: Think about the word 'interpret'

questions.text: What is the name of a sampling method where the researcher sets how many people of each type to include (for example 50 men and 50 women) and selects people until each group is filled? Give the term.
questions.solution: Quota sampling fills set numbers (quotas) of each type of person; it is quick but not random
questions.hint: Each group has a fixed number, called a ...

questions.text: What name is given to a study of the same group of people over a long period of time, collecting data at intervals? Give the term.
questions.solution: A longitudinal study follows the same people over years, showing changes over time
questions.hint: The study is 'long' in time

questions.text: A sociologist wants to study a gang's daily life in detail, and believes the gang would act differently if they knew they were being studied. Which method suits this aim?
questions.solution: Joining the gang secretly gives rich, valid data about real behaviour (though it raises ethical issues)
questions.hint: The gang must not know about the research

questions.text: A researcher wants to compare the views of 2,000 parents across the UK quickly and cheaply. Which method suits this aim?

options: An online or postal questionnaire with closed questions

questions.solution: Questionnaires can reach large samples cheaply and give quantitative data that is easy to compare
questions.hint: Which method works for a large number of people at low cost?

questions.text: A researcher chooses every 10th name from a school register. Which sampling method is this?
questions.solution: Systematic sampling picks every nth person from a sampling frame
questions.hint: There is a fixed pattern to the selection

questions.text: A researcher studying graffiti artists who do not want to be identified interviews one artist, who introduces the researcher to others, who introduce more. Which sampling method is this?
questions.solution: Snowball sampling uses contacts to reach hard-to-find groups; the sample grows like a rolling snowball
questions.hint: The sample grows bigger as it 'rolls' from one person to the next

questions.text: People being interviewed sometimes give answers that make them look good rather than true answers. What is this called? Give the term.
questions.solution: Social desirability bias: respondents give answers they think are acceptable, which reduces validity
questions.hint: People want to seem 'desirable' to society

questions.text: A researcher divides a population into groups, such as age groups, and then randomly samples from each group in proportion to its size. Which sampling method is this? Give the term.
questions.solution: Stratified sampling divides the population into layers (strata) and samples each in proportion, making the sample representative
questions.hint: The population is divided into layers, called strata

questions.text: A questionnaire was sent to 1,000 people and 150 replied. What is the response rate, and what is the main problem?

options: 15% — the people who replied may not be representative

questions.solution: 150 ÷ 1,000 = 15%. With a low response rate, those who reply may differ from those who don't, so the sample may be unrepresentative
questions.hint: Divide the replies by the number sent out, then think about who replied

questions.text: Which is a disadvantage of covert participant observation?

options: It raises ethical problems because the group has not given informed consent
The group knows it is being watched, so it changes its behaviour
It is cheap and quick to carry out
feedback: That is a problem with OVERT observation
Being cheap and quick would be an advantage

questions.solution: Covert research deceives the group, who cannot give informed consent; it can also be risky for the researcher
questions.hint: Think about ethics when the group does not know

questions.text: Factory workers became more productive whenever researchers changed their working conditions, even when the conditions got worse, because they knew they were being studied. Which effect does this describe?
questions.solution: The Hawthorne effect: people change their behaviour because they know they are being observed
questions.hint: It is named after the factory where it was first noticed

questions.text: A researcher uses questionnaires AND interviews in the same study to check the findings against each other. What is this called?
questions.solution: Triangulation uses more than one method so that the results can be cross-checked
questions.hint: Think of checking a position from more than one direction

questions.text: Which ethical principle means that participants' names and personal details must be kept private? Give the term.
questions.solution: Confidentiality (and anonymity) protects participants' identities and personal information
questions.hint: Information is kept secret, or 'confidential'

questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using unstructured interviews in sociological research.

rubric.model_answer: Advantage: unstructured interviews are flexible, like a guided conversation, so the interviewer can follow up interesting points and build rapport. This produces rich, detailed qualitative data with high validity, showing how people really see their lives. Disadvantage: each interview is different, so they are hard to repeat and compare, making them less reliable. They are also time-consuming, so samples are small and may not be representative, and the interviewer's presence may influence answers (interviewer bias).
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: advantage identified (e.g. flexible, rapport)
1 mark: advantage explained (e.g. rich, valid qualitative data)
1 mark: disadvantage identified (e.g. hard to compare, time-consuming)
1 mark: disadvantage explained (e.g. low reliability, small samples, interviewer bias)
(Maximum 4 marks)

questions.solution: Advantage: flexible, rich valid data. Disadvantage: hard to repeat or compare (less reliable) and time-consuming
questions.hint: Think about validity for the advantage and reliability for the disadvantage

questions.text: Which statement explains why positivists prefer questionnaires?

options: They allow the researcher to join in with the group
They produce rich, detailed qualitative data
They need no sampling at all
They produce standardised, quantitative data that can be checked for reliability

questions.solution: Questionnaires ask everyone the same questions, giving reliable, comparable numbers, which fits the positivist scientific approach
questions.hint: Positivists value reliability and numbers

questions.text: Why do interpretivists often criticise official statistics?

options: Statistics are socially constructed and may not show the meanings behind people's actions
Statistics are too detailed and qualitative
Statistics are collected by the researcher personally

questions.solution: Interpretivists say statistics are products of decisions by officials and do not reveal the meanings people give to events
questions.hint: Interpretivists care about meanings, not just numbers

questions.text: Which statement about reliability and validity is accurate?

options: Reliable research gives a true picture; valid research gives similar results when repeated
Reliable research gives similar results when repeated; valid research gives a true picture of what is studied
Reliability and validity mean exactly the same thing
Qualitative research is always more reliable than quantitative research
feedback: This has the two definitions the wrong way round

questions.solution: Reliability = consistency when repeated; validity = truthfulness or accuracy of the picture
questions.hint: One is about consistency, the other is about truth

questions.text: A researcher studies 20 pupils at one school and concludes that all UK teenagers think the same way. What is the main problem?

options: The study used too many methods
The sample is small and unrepresentative, so the results cannot be generalised

questions.solution: 20 pupils from one school are unlikely to represent all UK teenagers, so the findings cannot be generalised
questions.hint: Think about how many people were studied and where they came from

questions.text: What term describes how far research findings from a sample can be applied to the wider population? Give the term.

feedback.representativeness: Representativeness is whether the SAMPLE reflects the population — applying findings more widely is a related but different idea

questions.solution: Generalisability depends on a large, representative sample
questions.hint: The word describes being able to apply results 'in general'

questions.text: Evaluate the use of participant observation in sociological research.

rubric.model_answer: Participant observation lets the researcher see behaviour in its natural setting and understand the group's meanings, giving rich, valid qualitative data. Interpretivists favour it for this reason, and covert observation can reach hidden groups such as gangs. However, it is time-consuming, and usually only one small group is studied, so it is hard to generalise and impossible to repeat exactly (low reliability). The researcher may 'go native' and lose objectivity, and covert research raises ethical problems such as lack of informed consent and possible danger.
rubric.mark_scheme:
1 mark: strength identified (e.g. high validity, natural setting)
1 mark: strength explained (e.g. understands meanings, interpretivist view)
1 mark: weakness: low reliability or representativeness
1 mark: weakness: time, cost or going native
1 mark: ethical issues of covert observation
1 mark: a balanced judgement
(Maximum 6 marks)

questions.solution: Strengths: valid, detailed data about real behaviour. Weaknesses: unreliable, unrepresentative, time-consuming, ethical problems if covert
questions.hint: Weigh validity against reliability, representativeness and ethics
